newsitem.title: USA: Short-term cobalt tightness ruled out by industry.
newsitem.headline: Short-term cobalt tightness ruled out by industry.

text.p: Cobalt prices are set to firm slightly over the coming months and the gap between Western and Russian metal values should widen, but major tightness has been ruled out, traders and producers said.

"I don't see supply tightening, but the stockpile of cobalt is somewhere near 2,000 tonnes. That's less than one month's global inventory," Paul Helsel, president of trader firm Phoenixx International Resources, told the Gorham/Intertech cobalt conference in New York on Wednesday.
Cobalt processor Union Miniere said its joint venture project with Gecamines in Zaire to recover 3,000 tonnes of metal from the Kasombo mine would ease any tightness.
"It's a short-term project that is going to help to bridge any shortage gap," said Mark Caffarey, executive vice president of UM's U.S.-based Carolmet Cobalt Products.
Several delegates questioned why the price difference between Western higher grade cobalt and lower grade Russian material was less than $1 per pound.
"If demand for high grade metal is strong, the differential will be wider," said Edward Kielty, managing director of consumer Hall Chemical Co.
Helsel said there was greater acceptance of Russian metal, unlike four years ago, but the country was "inconsistent with their deliveries".

Rami Weissfisch of Minor Metals Inc said the market was in an unusual situation. "The supply of Russian for the last six to eight weeks have not been coming through. With less availability of Russian, the price of Russian material has been moving up, while high grade metal producers have been selling. What you see is temporary."

Helsel forecast that cobalt prices, currently around $22 to $23 per pound, will rise by at least $2 to $3 per pound within the next three months as consumers return from vacations. "The consumers in the United States are extremely disciplined - they will wait as long as they can."
Few delegates wished to see the return of African producer-led prices that were abandoned for published prices in trade journals and elsewhere.
"I don't think producer prices will come again - the free market price is not completely free, but it's the only system we have at the moment," Caffarey said.

Helsel said a London Metal Exchange cobalt futures contract would push the metal into the realm of precious metals, and relatively small cobalt stocks could easily be bought up and the market manipulated.
"There would not be enough volume to do that justice," Helsel said.

Traders are awaiting keenly the U.S. government stockpile's decision, due around the Cobalt Development Institute's conference in Pittsburgh next month, as to how stockpiled cobalt will be sold over the coming year.

Some traders have privately claimed that sales over the past year were priced on a formula linked to published prices. There were attempts to push published prices lower so stockpiled metal, once the tonnage was awarded, would be priced more cheaply, traders have said.

Stockpile administrator Richard Connelly declined to comment on pricing methods. "Rumor and speculation in this market remain rampant. Contracts will remain completely confidential," Connelly told delegates.
There are expectations that the stockpile may alter how future sales are priced.
